newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed disarms former enemy with message of peace.
newsitem.headline: Lebed disarms former enemy with message of peace.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed entered the nerve centre of NATO's military machine on Tuesday with a message of peace for Moscow's Cold War foe.

"The planet earth needs reason and intelligence and not wars. Let it be so," Lebed, for 20 years a soldier in the Warsaw Pact pitted against NATO, scrawled in the visitors' book at the alliance's command centre in southern Belgium.
U.S. General George Joulwan, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), wrote:
"Together, we can make it happen".

The exchange was typical of the moderate tone that Lebed has adopted during a two-day visit to NATO's political and military headquarters in stark contrast to previous outbursts over the alliance plans to expand eastwards.
At times, Lebed's first trip to the West has appeared more like that of a head of state, with both hosts and guests avoiding controversy and clearly trying to get to know each other better.
Lebed, President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser, is a strong candidate to succeed him if he has to bow out of office due to ill health.

A 46-year-old ex-paratroop general, Lebed has clearly enjoyed his high-level reception. On Monday, he met NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and addressed the alliance's 16 ambassadors on the future of Russia-NATO relations.

After being greeted by Joulwan at the entrance to the alliance's sprawling military complex of two-storey buildings, Lebed stood smartly to attention near a NATO banner and Russian flag as a military band played the Russian national anthem.

Lebed, dressed in civilian clothes but with his military bearing plain to see, walked slowly along an inspection line of soldiers from allied countries ranging from Turkey in the south to Norway in the north.

Before moving inside the sprawling complex, where in former days the defeat of the Soviet Union was planned, the two men signed the official visitors' book in front of a backdrop of the flags of all 16 NATO allies.

Throughout the visit, Lebed has studiously avoided any repetition of earlier colourful tirades against the alliance which he has accused of behaving like a "drunken hooligan" in its haste to expand into former communist territory.
Playing the statesman, Lebed has limited himself to saying he hopes enlargement can be postponed for a generation to allow the bitterness of the Cold War to fade.

He persisted with the moderate line on Tuesday. After meeting the Secretary-General of the Western European Union (WEU) Jose Cutileiro, he said a civilised West would not seek to threaten Russia and dialogue would continue.
"We will find an agreement in a civilised manner," he told reporters.
Cutileiro, echoing comments of NATO's ambassadors on Monday, said he had found Lebed "well-informed, precise and open".
Lebed and Joulwan were also expected to visit the control room for the alliance-led peace mission in Bosnia.
Russia has about 2,000 troops in the 55,000-strong force and a Russian liaison officer occupies an office next to Joulwan in an unprecedented show of post-Cold War cooperation.

Solana has proposed assigning Russian liaison officers at virtually all levels of the alliance's command structure in order to quell Moscow's fears of expansion as part of a new charter governing all aspects of NATO-Russia relations.

NATO says a new pact with Russia could run in parallel with plans to take in new members from central and eastern Europe, probably starting with Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic, but rejects Moscow's attempts to link the two issues.
Before leaving for Mons, Lebed paid a brief courtesy visit on Belgium's Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet.
Asked about a renewed campaign against his Chechnya peace deal, apparently timed to coincide with his absence from the country, Lebed dismissed the criticism as insignificant.
"The dog barks and the caravan passes," he growled in his now-familiar deep voice.
